items.followUp: State five postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory.

rubric.why: Identifies the allowed paths in which electrons revolve around the nucleus.
rubric.description: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain permitted circular orbits or shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons revolve in allowed orbits or shells.

rubric.why: States that each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
rubric.description: Each permitted orbit has a definite, fixed energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the energy of an allowed orbit is fixed or definite.

rubric.why: States that electrons do not exchange energy while remaining in an allowed orbit.
rubric.description: An electron does not emit or absorb energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an electron does not emit or absorb energy in an allowed orbit.

rubric.why: Describes energy absorption or emission when an electron changes orbits.
rubric.description: An electron absorbs or emits energy when it jumps from one orbit to another; the energy change is ΔE = hν.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking a jump between orbits with absorption or emission of energy.

rubric.why: States Bohr’s quantisation condition for electron angular momentum.
rubric.description: The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantised: mvr = nh/2π.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that angular momentum is quantised or giving the relation mvr = nh/2π.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain permitted circular paths called orbits or shells.
Each permitted orbit has a definite, fixed energy.
An electron does not emit or absorb energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
An electron absorbs or emits energy when it jumps from one orbit to another; the energy change is ΔE = hν.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantised: mvr = nh/2π.

items.followUp: Describe the steps used to write the chemical formula of calcium nitrate.

rubric.why: Identifies the ions and places the positive ion before the negative ion.
rubric.description: Write the formulae of the positive and negative ions, with the positive ion first.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the positive and negative ions and writing the positive ion first.

rubric.why: Uses the valency of each ion as the basis for the subscripts.
rubric.description: Write the valency of each ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating or showing that the valencies of both ions are written.

rubric.why: Applies the criss-cross method to make the valencies subscripts.
rubric.description: Criss-cross the valencies to become subscripts of the other ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing or applying the criss-cross method.

rubric.why: States how to simplify the subscripts and handle a polyatomic ion when needed.
rubric.description: Reduce the subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio; use brackets around a polyatomic ion if its subscript is greater than one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the simplification rule and/or correct bracket use for a polyatomic ion.

modelAnswer: Write the symbols or formulae of the positive and negative ions, with the positive ion first.
Write the valency of each ion.
Criss-cross the valencies to become subscripts of the other ion.
Reduce the subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio; use brackets around a polyatomic ion if its subscript is greater than one.
For example, Ca²⁺ and NO₃⁻ give Ca(NO₃)₂.

items.followUp: Define hydrogen bonding and explain its role in the properties of water.

rubric.why: Defines hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular attraction involving hydrogen bonded to an electronegative atom.
rubric.description: Hydrogen bonding is a weak intermolecular attraction involving a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom and an electronegative atom of another molecule.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for identifying the attraction as intermolecular and describing the relevant hydrogen–electronegative atom arrangement.

rubric.why: Identifies the atoms involved and the attraction to an electronegative atom on a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.description: Hydrogen is bonded to F, O, or N and is attracted to a lone pair on F, O, or N in a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for identifying H–F, H–O, or H–N and the neighbouring atom/lone pair involved.

rubric.why: Explains hydrogen bonding between water molecules as an example.
rubric.description: In water, the partially positive hydrogen atom of one H₂O molecule is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atom of another H₂O molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct water example showing the attraction between neighbouring molecules.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is a weak intermolecular attraction involving a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom and an electronegative atom of another molecule.
It occurs when hydrogen is bonded to fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen and is attracted to a lone pair on F, O, or N in a neighbouring molecule.
In water, the partially positive hydrogen atom of one H₂O molecule is attracted to the partially negative oxygen atom of another H₂O molecule.
This attraction between neighbouring water molecules is a hydrogen bond.

items.followUp: Compare a true solution and a colloid using particle size, settling, and the Tyndall effect.

rubric.why: Compares the relative sizes of suspension and colloidal particles.
rubric.description: Suspension particles are larger than colloidal particles; colloidal particles are approximately 1–1000 nm in size.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct comparison of particle sizes or the colloid size range.

rubric.why: Contrasts whether particles settle on standing.
rubric.description: Suspension particles settle on standing, whereas colloidal particles remain dispersed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting settling behaviour.

rubric.why: Compares how the two types of particles behave during ordinary filtration.
rubric.description: Suspension particles can be separated by ordinary filtration; colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting filtration behaviour.

rubric.why: Identifies the light-scattering behaviour of colloids.
rubric.description: Colloids scatter light and show the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying light scattering or the Tyndall effect in colloids.

modelAnswer: Suspension particles are larger than colloidal particles; colloidal particles are approximately 1–1000 nm in size.
Suspension particles settle on standing, whereas colloidal particles remain dispersed.
Suspension particles can be separated by ordinary filtration; colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper.
Colloids scatter light and show the Tyndall effect.

items.followUp: Define a mixture and give one example.

rubric.why: Defines a compound as a pure substance made from elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion.
rubric.description: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that elements are chemically combined in a fixed proportion.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a compound.
rubric.description: Water (H₂O), sodium chloride (NaCl), and carbon dioxide (CO₂) are examples of compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct compound example, with or without its formula.

modelAnswer: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Water (H₂O) is an example of a compound.
